flashcards.q: What happens to false-positive rate when you repeatedly peek at a fixed-horizon A/B test's p-value before its planned end?
flashcards.a: It inflates from the nominal ~5% to commonly cited estimates above 25% -- roughly one in four calls made this way is noise, not signal, because each look is an implicit additional hypothesis test.

flashcards.q: Name three fixes for the peeking problem, in order of how commonly they're implemented.
flashcards.a: 1) Lock the dashboard until the pre-committed sample size is reached (purely procedural). 2) Alpha-spending functions (pre-declared interim-analysis schedule, e.g. O'Brien-Fleming or Pocock). 3) Always-valid p-values / confidence sequences (mSPRT-based), valid at every sample size, safe to check continuously.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between the novelty effect and the primacy effect?
flashcards.a: Novelty effect: users respond MORE positively to a variant simply because it's new (a false positive that decays over days-weeks). Primacy effect (change aversion): users respond MORE negatively at first because they're accustomed to the old way (a false negative that recovers as they adjust).

flashcards.q: Why does a high-returning-traffic surface (SaaS product UI) need a longer test runtime than a high-new-visitor surface to catch novelty effects?
flashcards.a: On a high-new-visitor surface, most users see the change for the first time regardless of variant, so there's little novelty differential. On a high-returning-traffic surface, most of the treatment arm experiences a genuine change from an established habit, so novelty/primacy effects can be large and take weeks to wash out.

flashcards.q: How do you catch novelty/primacy decay concretely, rather than just running longer arbitrarily?
flashcards.a: Segment analysis by new-vs-returning traffic and by exposure count (1st vs Nth visit post-launch) within returning users -- a flattening or reversing trend as exposure count grows is the signature of decaying novelty/primacy, and it tells you when the effect has actually stabilized rather than guessing a fixed extra week.

flashcards.q: What is a holdback/haircut group and why use one even after a test has already 'won'?
flashcards.a: A small permanent control group kept running after a winning variant ships to 100% of remaining traffic, specifically to catch a lift that was partly or wholly novelty-driven and fades over subsequent weeks -- the most reliable way to confirm a launch decision was actually correct, reserved for high-stakes, hard-to-reverse launches.

flashcards.q: Why is 'no statistically significant difference' NOT the same claim as 'the feature has no effect'?
flashcards.a: A null result only rules out effects larger than the test's achieved MDE at the collected sample size -- it says nothing about smaller, still-meaningful effects the test wasn't powered to detect. Always report the achieved MDE alongside a null result.

flashcards.q: What is multiple-metric fishing and how is it the same underlying problem as peeking?
flashcards.a: Running one test but checking many metrics and reporting whichever crossed significance -- the same multiple-comparisons inflation as peeking, just applied across metrics instead of across time. Fix: pre-register ONE primary metric; treat other movements as directional/exploratory only.

flashcards.q: What's an always-valid p-value (mSPRT) and why do modern experimentation platforms default to it?
flashcards.a: A significance test constructed so Type I error is controlled simultaneously at every sample size, so looking any number of times -- including continuously -- never inflates the false-positive rate. Platforms default to it because users will look at live dashboards early and often regardless of documented warnings, so the correction is built into the statistic itself.

flashcards.q: What's the single cheapest, highest-value automated check every A/B test should have before its result is trusted?
flashcards.a: An automated sample ratio mismatch (SRM) check -- a chi-squared test on observed vs expected arm counts, run before any metric is displayed, hard-blocking the report if triggered. It's a few lines of code and catches the most common real-world experiment-invalidating bug. (Full root-cause treatment: T32-experiment-design.)
